piece.title: How to reduce no-shows: 9 tactics that work
piece.status: draft refresh of a published post

sections.heading: (intro)
paragraphs: A missed appointment is an empty chair you can't sell twice. For a salon, a clinic or a studio, a few no-shows a week add up to a lost day every month, and the client who didn't come often doesn't rebook either.

We looked at 199,640 appointments across 1,240 businesses that use online booking. When no reminder was sent, 11.9% of appointments ended as no-shows. With reminders turned on, the rate fell to 6.4%. Here are the nine tactics that made the difference, starting with the cheapest.

sections.heading: Why no-shows happen
paragraphs: Most clients who miss an appointment simply forgot. They booked weeks ago, the day got busy, and nothing reminded them. A smaller group meant to cancel but found it awkward to call, so they didn't. A few never planned to come.

Most clients prefer a text reminder over an email, because a text gets read within minutes and an email can sit unopened until the evening. That matters when the reminder is your last chance to fill the slot.

The cost is real. The Example Practice Managers Association's 2025 survey put the cost of one missed clinic appointment at $85, before counting the client who drifts away. Each of the tactics below goes after one of these causes: forgetting, awkwardness or a lack of commitment.

sections.heading: Tactic 1: Send reminders, and time them well
paragraphs: A reminder is the cheapest fix there is, but timing changes how much it helps. Send it too early and people forget again; send it too late and they can't rearrange their day or tell you in time to rebook the slot.

In the study, every business sent one SMS reminder, at a time each business picked. Reminders sent 72 hours ahead had a no-show rate of 8.1%. Reminders sent 48 hours ahead had a no-show rate of 6.6%. At 24 hours the rate was 4.9%, the lowest of the five. At 12 hours it was 5.5%, and a reminder only 2 hours ahead left 7.1%.
If you only send one reminder, send it the day before. If you send two, add a short one on the morning of the appointment with a one-tap link to confirm or cancel.

sections.heading: Tactic 2: Turn on reminders in your booking settings
paragraphs: In Example Booking Software, open Settings and choose Reminders. Switch on SMS reminders, set the first reminder to 24 hours before the appointment, and tick Add a confirm or cancel link. Then click Save. Reminders go out from the next booking onward; appointments already on the calendar get them too.
Check the message text before you save. Keep the business name, the date and time, and the link. Cut anything else, because a long text gets skimmed and the link is the part that matters.

sections.heading: Tactic 3: Take a deposit
paragraphs: A deposit turns a booking into a commitment. Clients who have paid something show up, and the ones who can't make it tell you, because they want the deposit moved to a new date.
Businesses that started taking deposits cut no-shows by 70% within six months. In the month before, 12.4% of their appointments were no-shows.
Keep the deposit small enough that it doesn't put new clients off: a flat amount for short services, a share of the price for long ones. Say clearly when it is refunded and when it isn't.

sections.heading: Tactics 4 to 9: Confirm, follow up and fill the gaps
paragraphs: The remaining six tactics work as one sequence, from the moment someone books to the moment you fill a slot they left. Set it up once and it runs on its own.

First, the booking is confirmed on screen. Second, a confirmation email goes out with the details and a calendar file. Third, a reminder arrives 24 hours ahead. Fourth, a short reminder comes 2 hours ahead with a confirm or cancel link. Fifth, if the client doesn't show, a follow-up message offers a new time the same day.
Sixth, keep a waitlist. When someone cancels through the link, the slot is offered to the first person on the waitlist, so a late cancellation still becomes a booking instead of a gap.

How do the main options compare? Reminders take minutes to set up and cost the client nothing. A deposit takes an hour to set up and asks the client to pay a little upfront. A cancellation fee takes about the same time, costs the client only if they miss, and needs a written policy. A waitlist takes minutes and costs the client nothing. Most businesses start with reminders, then add a deposit for their longest services.

Whatever you choose, write it down in a short policy and show it at the moment of booking. Clients accept rules they saw before they booked; they argue with rules they meet afterward. Keep the policy to a few lines, use plain words, and repeat the key line in every reminder so nobody can say they didn't know.

Review the numbers once a month. Look at no-shows by service and by day of the week, and move the stricter rules to the slots that miss most. A Saturday morning slot that is missed often deserves a deposit; a Tuesday afternoon slot that is rarely missed may not.

sections.heading: No-show rates by industry
paragraphs: Reminders helped in every industry in the study, but not by the same amount. Salons went from 12.6% without reminders to 5.3% with them. Clinics went from 10.5% without reminders to 6.1% with them. Fitness studios went from 14.3% without reminders to 8.2% with them. Personal trainers went from 9.5% without reminders to 6.7% with them.
The gap is widest where appointments are booked far ahead and easy to forget, and narrowest where clients already see the trainer every week.

sections.heading: Start with one change this week
paragraphs: If you do one thing, turn on a reminder 24 hours ahead. Across the study it took the no-show rate from 11.9% to 6.4%. Then add a deposit for the services that miss most, and let the waitlist fill what's left.
